item.title: 6 Strategies to Curb Impulsive Spending
item.description:
Impulse Control Disorders

6 Strategies to Curb Impulsive Spending

Engaging in retail therapy that you later regret? Here's what to do.

Posted September 25, 2026

Key points
  • Impulsive spending involves making spontaneous, emotionally driven purchases.
  • Those struggling with emotion dysregulation and poor executive functioning have higher risk for impulse buys.
  • Skills and strategies from Dialectical Behavior Therapy can help prevent impulsive spending.
Source: Kendel Media / pexels

You are scrolling on your phone after a particularly stressful day when the ads start gliding by. The world’s softest pair of sweatpants, and they are on sale! A set of kettle bells that glow in the dark for your next disco workout. A slick, glossy polish that supposedly won’t wreck your nails (and if you buy three sets you won’t have to pay for shipping). After just a few taps, the items are in your cart, ready for check out.

Impulsive Versus Compulsive Spending

The urge to buy sometimes comes on so suddenly and strongly that it feels nearly impossible to resist. Some researchers make the distinction between impulsive versus compulsive spending. Impulsive spending is defined as spontaneous and emotionally driven, while compulsive spending is defined as more chronic in nature and leading to significant distress. Both, however, involve difficulties with self-regulation and can lead to lower well-being and financial hardship.

Risk Factors for Purchasing on a Whim

Compulsive buying has been increasing in prevalence over recent decades. Certain individuals seem to be more susceptible, including younger adults and individuals with difficulty problem solving, planning, and resisting distractions. One study found that adverse childhood experiences–such as experiencing abuse or neglect–were associated with emotion regulation problems and anxiety, each of which were also associated with impulsive spending. Another study similarly found that emotion dysregulation and impulsivity accounted for a relationship between childhood trauma and impulsive spending.

Although anyone can struggle with making purchases that are not thoroughly considered, certain mental health diagnoses are associated with impulsive spending. Research suggests that individuals with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are more susceptible to making impulsive purchases and having trouble delaying gratification, and impulsive or uncontrollable spending is included in the diagnostic criteria for bipolar disorder and borderline personality disorder.

Strategies for Curbing Impulsive Spending

If you are struggling with impulse purchases, try these six strategies from dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) to prevent buyer’s remorse:

  1. Reflect on what led to a past impulsive purchase. Completing a chain analysis on a past impulsive purchase can help you come to a deeper understanding of what led to a seemingly out-of-the blue decision. Think back to the prompting event for the purchase. This could have been merchandise-related, like seeing an Instagram posting from an influencer who looked great in what they were wearing. But it could also be an emotionally charged event, like a fight with a loved one that left you feeling unsettled and sent you towards retail therapy. It can also be helpful to reflect on vulnerability factors that preceded the prompting event and made you more susceptible to the purchase, like recently getting your paycheck or feeling emotionally drained from a tough week. After you have identified a prompting event and vulnerability factors, write out everything that happened between the prompting event and making a purchase, whether that was an action you took, a thought that went through your mind, or an emotion that you felt. For example, did you check to see whether Afterpay was available (action)? Did you imagine yourself showing up to work in that new outfit (thought)? Did you feel a rush of pleasure at the idea of how good you would look (emotion)? Each of the steps in the chain towards clicking “purchase” is an opportunity to intervene and prevent an impulsive buy in the future.
  2. Write out the short- and long-term consequences of your last impulsive purchase. Short-term consequences can be positive or negative, like enjoying the anticipation of waiting for the package to arrive, a further spark of joy when unboxing the item, or feeling guilty that you didn’t save anything from this month’s paycheck. Long-term consequences may be primarily negative with an impulsive purchase, like the cheap sweater eventually pilling so much that you stop wearing it, the headphones getting replaced by a newer model and ending up in a landfill, or a purchase contributing to growing credit card debt.
  3. Write out the pros and cons before making a purchase. Once you have clicked “add to cart” (or have literally put an item in your real-life shopping cart), but before you enter your credit card details or fork over cash, write out a list of pros and cons for buying the item. Yes, that is going to be cumbersome. However, it will slow down your process of making the purchase and force you to deliberately weigh the decision.
  4. Reflect on whether you are trying to avoid a particular emotion. We often seek quick happiness because we are trying to escape another feeling: disappointment, boredom, anxiety, or despair. A purchase isn’t going to fix that emotion, we are ultimately just delaying it. Consider mindfully allowing yourself to experience the emotion, even just for a few minutes, before deciding whether or not to make the purchase.
  5. Use another way to self-soothe. Sometimes an emotion is so strong that we need a way to soothe ourselves. Luckily, shopping is not the only option. Our five senses can each be a helpful portal to self-soothing, particularly when used in combination. For example, tidy your favorite corner of the house and sit there under pleasant lamplight (sight). Put on music that speaks to your soul, whether that is jazz, bluegrass, classical, or lo-fi (sound). Make yourself mint tea or slice some fresh fruit (taste), light fragrant candles (smell), and slip into soft, dryer-warm pajamas (touch).
  6. Accept reality as it is. Effective advertising persuades us that we can escape reality and discover a new version of ourselves. This is what makes purchases so alluring — we can’t help but want those new glasses when we think about the type of person we will be while wearing them. The best way to combat this mirage? Accepting reality, which means accepting ourselves and our lives as we are currently living them. Accepting reality doesn’t mean we can’t change it. But the kind of change we are seeking doesn’t usually come through one more purchase.

item.title: How Infertility Changes the Story You Tell About Yourself
item.description:
Infertility

How Infertility Changes the Story You Tell About Yourself

How infertility can reshape self-worth and the way you see yourself.

Posted September 25, 2026

Key points
  • Infertility can gradually change the way you see yourself and your future.
  • Psychologists have described infertility as a narcissistic injury: a blow to self-esteem and identity.
  • Shame and self-blame can turn a reproductive struggle into the conclusion that something is wrong with you.
  • Research on infertility-related complex PTSD (cPTSD) points to a persistent negative self-concept.

Infertility becomes personal
Source: Envato/Westend61

At the start, you probably approached infertility the way you would approach any other medical problem. You booked the tests, picked up a new vocabulary of follicle counts and protocols, and waited for someone to tell you what was wrong and how to fix it.

If you went through several cycles, you may know how the questions start to change. Instead of asking why a treatment failed, you begin wondering what is wrong with you. A negative beta test lands as a judgment about who you are. Your body can start to feel unreliable or even like it is working against you.

“I thought if I just did everything right, it would work.” That was how one client described her first year of fertility treatment (details have been changed). By her fourth failed transfer, she no longer said, “The treatment didn’t work.” She said, “I couldn’t do it.” What had changed was where she located the failure. Instead of seeing the treatment as unsuccessful, she had started to see herself that way.

Infertility puts the hope of a child at risk. It also chips away at assumptions you may never have had to think about: that your body would cooperate, and that parenthood would come more or less when you felt ready.

Infertility as a Narcissistic Injury

Psychologists use the idea of narcissistic injury to describe what infertility can do to your sense of self.

In this context, the term “narcissistic” does not mean self-absorbed. It refers to an injury to your self-esteem and identity, and to your beliefs about how your life was supposed to unfold.

Irving Leon described infertility as a narcissistic injury because it challenges several of these beliefs simultaneously. More recent research frames it as a blow to generative identity, your sense of yourself as someone who can create a family.

When generative identity is shaken, the way you talk about treatment can change. You might have caught yourself saying "I failed" after a cancelled cycle, or "My body is broken" after a poor response to medication. Thoughts like these tend to feel like plain facts, with little awareness that they are interpretations.

From Uncertainty to Self-Blame

Searching for Meaning in Infertility
Source: Envato/MikeShots

People look for meaning in what happens to them. An explanation makes a painful experience easier to understand and can offer some sense of control.

Infertility rarely gives you one. There may be no satisfying reason a transfer failed, a pregnancy ended, or a friend conceived within two months of trying. Even a clear diagnosis answers the medical question while leaving the personal one untouched: "Why is this happening to me?"

When no explanation holds, you may have supplied your own, and the easiest one to reach for is usually yourself. "What caused this?" becomes "What is wrong with me?" Each unsuccessful treatment can then feel like more evidence that your body cannot be trusted.

Self-blame can take hold even when the medical evidence points elsewhere. A man whose partner had been through three rounds of IVF kept replaying his twenties, wondering whether his drinking or his cycling had caused their male-factor diagnosis, as he described himself as "the reason we're here."

Shame deepens this process. Someone can know rationally that infertility is not a personal failing and still feel that it is. Watching others have children without any struggles reinforces the sense of falling short of something that was supposed to come naturally.

Once the problem feels located in the self, it can reach into how feminine or masculine a person feels, how comfortable they are in their body, and their experience of sexuality. It can also change how much they allow others to see what infertility has changed in their lives.

That silence has its own effect. Beliefs that are never spoken aloud aren't questioned, so they tend to persist over time.

When Trauma Changes Self-Perception

When Trauma Changes the Way You See Yourself
Source: Envato/MaxBelchenko

Recent research on infertility-related trauma adds another dimension.

A 2026 study in Human Reproduction found that among participants who described their infertility experience as traumatic, 9% met criteria for PTSD while 32% met criteria for complex PTSD (cPTSD).

CPTSD includes the core symptoms of PTSD along with difficulties regulating emotions, strain in relationships, and a persistent negative self-concept. In this sample, that self-concept showed up as feelings of inadequacy, low self-esteem, self-blame, and hostility towards the body.

These findings connect to narcissistic injury and shame. Repeated loss, failed treatment, and a long stretch of helplessness can create fear about what lies ahead. They can also confirm beliefs about the self that began forming much earlier in the process.

If infertility felt traumatic for you, healing may mean working with two things: the memories of what happened, and the conclusions you drew about yourself along the way.

What Infertility Can Leave Behind

Infertility can change how you see yourself, and that change does not necessarily end when treatment does.

A diagnosis can shape how you relate to your body for years. Repeated disappointment can plant self-doubt in parts of life that once felt secure.

A positive pregnancy test or a live birth does not automatically undo these beliefs. Many people who become parents after infertility are surprised to find the old self-judgment still in place.

Infertility may eventually stop being something you are going through. The story it taught you about yourself can remain long after.

item.title: When a Partner Lacks the Gift of Perspective-Taking
item.description:
Emotional Intelligence

When a Partner Lacks the Gift of Perspective-Taking

Emotionally intelligent people need to see when a partner does not reciprocate.

Posted September 25, 2026

Key points
  • Emotionally intelligent people naturally take on different perspectives.
  • Some partners do not perspective-take and label you antagonistic when you are fighting to be understood.
  • Recognizing your partner's emotional unavailability allows you to believe in yourself.

As an emotionally intelligent person, you tend to think and care about how you impact other people. You dislike seeing other people hurt, so you do your best to be inclusive and conscientious. To understand people better, you try to see things from their viewpoint for a moment, even when they feel differently. This perspective-taking ability may be so automatic that you may not even be aware that you do it. Also, you may assume that everybody does it. But some do not, especially in an interpersonal relationship when being close requires them to be authentically vulnerable. Instead, they may seem to always need to be right, perhaps to maintain the upper hand in the relationship.

Although it is hard to believe, there is a certain type of person who is too insecure to take a person’s perspective if it differs from their own in a close relationship. They may be able to contemplate a different viewpoint in the outside world because things are less personal, but in a close relationship, their self-esteem may not be strong enough to allow them to be wrong, so they dig in their heels. 

You, on the other hand, care more about understanding a loved one than being right, so you try your best to take a moment to see things from their vantage point. You want to understand them even if it means there is a possibility that you may be wrong. Your sense of self is strong enough to handle being incorrect, if you are. Essentially, you can handle it because it allows you to grow, know more about your loved one, yourself, and the situation. It also means that you are accountable in a relationship and are a safe person to talk to.

If you are in a relationship and you are brave enough to open up and say how you feel, but you are met with continual dismissals and admonishments, or you are overpowered, you may be struggling to be heard by someone who is not willing to listen because they are too insecure to be wrong. They present as if they are absolutely and completely positive that their perspective is superior to yours.

When you are fighting to be understood by someone who refuses to authentically consider your perspective because you feel differently from how they want you to feel, your healthy attempts to be close may be misconstrued as argumentative and antagonistic. This can add to confusion, and you may be so exhausted by the struggle that you start censoring how you feel, which results in the relationship feeling mechanical and unsatisfying.

Although it is a loss, it may help to accept that the person who you once felt close to may be unable to sustain the closeness that you once shared because of their own insecurities. Knowing how to proceed may require you to seek out additional resources on how to cope with an emotionally unavailable partner. You can find more information on this topic in my book, Loving Well: The Key to Satisfying and Joyful Relationships.
